2272.articleTitle: Benefits of Strength Training in Menopause and Beyond
2272.articleBodyCopy:
As we move through perimenopause and beyond, estrogen levels drop, affecting muscle strength, bone density, and metabolism. This can lead to weight gain, weaker bones, and a higher risk of injury. But strength training can help counteract these effects, keeping muscles strong, bones dense, and metabolism steady.

Lifting weights, using resistance bands, or even doing bodyweight exercises can make a big difference. Strength training also improves balance and joint stability, reducing the risk of falls. Plus, it’s not just about gym workouts—everyday items like a gallon of milk can work as makeshift weights. Staying strong doesn’t have to be complicated, but it sure does pay off!

2275.articleBodyCopy:
Menopause brings plenty of surprises, and unfortunately, more UTIs can be one of them. As estrogen levels drop, our good bacteria (lactobacillus) also decrease, making it easier for bad bacteria to take over. This change, along with a higher vaginal pH and thinning tissues, puts us at greater risk for infections. But here’s the kicker—sometimes, those UTI symptoms aren’t actually from an infection at all. Tight or irritated pelvic floor muscles can mimic UTIs, causing urgency, burning, and discomfort without any bacteria involved.

So how do you know the difference? A doctor can run a urine culture test to confirm if an infection is present—if not, your pelvic floor might be the real culprit. The good news is that pelvic floor therapy can help relax those muscles and reduce symptoms. If it is a UTI, medication will get you back on track. Either way, menopause doesn’t have to mean constant bathroom trips—there are ways to keep your bladder happy!

2276.articleTitle: Pelvic Floor Symptoms in Perimenopause: Why Now??
2276.articleBodyCopy:
Perimenopause can be a confusing time, especially when you suddenly start dealing with pelvic floor issues you didn’t experience before. Many women notice leaking, pressure, prolapse, or painful intimacy after years of being symptom-free. So, what’s going on? As estrogen levels decrease, the pelvic floor muscles can weaken, and the body may no longer be able to compensate for imbalances that were already there. Think of it as the “final straw” that triggers these issues.

The good news is you’re not stuck with these symptoms. Pelvic floor therapy can help identify what’s going on and put you on the path to recovery. Strengthening your pelvic floor muscles will improve function and reduce symptoms, leaving you feeling stronger and more comfortable. If you’ve been dealing with these issues, it’s time to give your pelvic floor some TLC with therapy!

2277.articleTitle: Prolapse Symptoms After Prolapse Repair Surgery
2277.articleBodyCopy:
Have you had prolapse repair surgery in the past, only to feel like those annoying symptoms are creeping back in? If you're in your 40s or 50s and experiencing pelvic floor symptoms like leaking, pressure, or heaviness, you're not alone. Here's the thing: your body’s going through a lot of changes right now, and some of those old symptoms might resurface due to hormonal shifts, especially estrogen levels during perimenopause and menopause.

But don't panic! The good news is that surgery alone isn't always the full solution. If you were never referred to pelvic floor therapy after your surgery, you might have missed out on learning techniques like proper pressure management, core bracing, and breath mechanics—all of which can play a major role in preventing symptoms from coming back. It's never too late to start strengthening your pelvic floor and learning how to better manage pressure, so you can keep living life confidently during this stage of your journey.

2278.articleTitle: Pressure Management During Exercise and Daily Life
2278.articleBodyCopy:
Our pelvic floor is often the unsung hero of our body—helping support everything from our organs to our posture. But did you know that the way you breathe plays a huge role in how well it functions? When you inhale, your diaphragm flattens and moves downward, pushing pressure into your abdominal and pelvic areas. The pelvic floor, in turn, lengthens to absorb that pressure. When you exhale, the pelvic floor springs back up, helping to support your organs and assisting the diaphragm as it pushes the air out of your lungs. This “piston” effect keeps your body functioning at its best, especially during movement and exercise.

As you go through perimenopause, changes in estrogen can make it harder to maintain pelvic floor strength, but don’t worry—simple breathing techniques can make a big difference. For example, when you’re doing squats or deadlifts, try exhaling during the harder part of the movement—like standing back up. This helps activate your pelvic floor and core muscles, ensuring that they work in harmony. The same technique can be applied to daily tasks, like picking up heavy laundry or your toddler. Remember: when in doubt, blow it out! This simple breathing hack will help support your pelvic floor and keep you feeling strong through your day.

2279.articleBodyCopy:
Ladies, let’s get real about pelvic floor health, especially as we enter perimenopause. You might have heard of kegels—those pelvic floor squeezes that are supposed to strengthen our muscles and fix everything from leaking to pelvic pain. Well, here’s the kicker: they might not be what you need right now. As estrogen levels drop during perimenopause, your pelvic floor muscles often become tighter, not weaker. So, if you’re squeezing away with kegels, you could actually be making things worse by adding more tension to an already overworked area.

Instead of focusing on kegels, it’s time to rethink how we approach pelvic floor care. Learning to relax your pelvic floor and practice proper breathing is key. Plus, adding strength training exercises like squats, lunges, and deadlifts (done with the right breathing technique, of course) can help your pelvic floor and the rest of your body work in harmony. A pelvic floor therapist can give you a personalized plan to tackle those pesky symptoms and get your pelvic muscles back on track. Forget about those stoplight squeezes—let’s build strength and muscle the right way!

2280.articleBodyCopy:
Perimenopause is a bit like that rollercoaster ride you never wanted to be on—up and down with your hormones, mood swings, and sleep struggles. But what if I told you there’s something you can do right now to make those upcoming changes a little easier to handle? That’s right—it's all about building muscle mass, and trust me, it’s not just for bodybuilders!

Here’s the deal: as you head into perimenopause, your estrogen starts to decline. When that happens, it doesn’t just mess with your mood, it also leads to a decrease in muscle mass. But don’t panic! If you start strength training now—especially lifting heavy weights—you can build up muscle mass before estrogen drops off for good. Think of it like saving up for a rainy day. By the time you hit menopause, you’ll have that solid muscle base to carry you through, keeping your body strong, healthy, and able to handle those pesky symptoms.

The best part? If you're already in menopause, it’s not too late. You can still build muscle! Grab those dumbbells or head to the gym for some serious strength training. Whether you’re just starting or already in the thick of it, it’s never too late to get stronger and feel better.

2281.articleTitle: 3 Tips for a Happy Pelvic Floor Health
2281.articleBodyCopy:
As we navigate perimenopause and menopause, pelvic floor health can be affected by changes in estrogen levels, leading to issues like bladder leaks, vaginal dryness, and painful intimacy. Dr. Becky Allen suggests using topical estrogen cream, which targets these tissues directly and can help improve symptoms quickly. Applying it to the inner labia and vaginal canal allows it to work locally where it’s needed most, promoting better tissue integrity and pelvic floor function.

In addition to the cream, strength training is key to maintaining muscle mass as estrogen declines. Lifting heavy weights helps build strong glutes, a solid core, and a well-functioning pelvic floor. Don’t forget the power of walking! Regular walking helps maintain pelvic floor mobility by lengthening and shortening muscles with each step, keeping them healthy and flexible. These three tips—estrogen cream, strength training, and walking—are simple yet effective ways to stay proactive about pelvic floor health during this phase of life.

2284.articleBodyCopy: Heart disease doesn’t always come with a big, dramatic warning sign—especially for women. We’re more likely to brush off the subtle stuff: fatigue, nausea, a little shortness of breath. But those quiet signals could mean something serious. If you’ve ever thought “It’s probably nothing,” this one’s for you. Your body might be whispering… and it’s time to listen.

2287.articleTitle: What Joy Does For Your Body (and Why it Matters)
2287.articleBodyCopy: When we engage in things that bring us joy, it supports not just our mental health, but our immune system too. We’re diving into what joy actually does for your health (hint: it’s more powerful than you think) and why the basics—movement, hydration, and time in nature—matter more now than ever. These aren't just “feel-good” habits—they’re biologically essential for energy, mood regulation, and long-term resilience. Choose something joyful from each category—movement, hydration, and nature—and explore how to bring more of it into your daily routine. Your body and brain will thank you. Study cited in the video: Ulrich, R. S. (1984). View through a window may influence recovery from surgery. Science, 224(4647), 420–421.

2288.articleBodyCopy:
Neuroplasticity isn’t just for babies learning to crawl—it’s for you, too. Our brains can rewire and adapt throughout our entire lives, not just in childhood. In fact, research shows that adults can create new neural pathways by trying new things, solving problems in fresh ways, and shaking up daily routines.

A fixed mindset shuts down possibilities and ramps up stress. And when we're stressed, our brains default to fight-or-flight mode. But when we embrace a growth mindset and stay open and adaptable, we train our brains to see more options and calm the nervous system. Practicing neuroplasticity is like cross-training for your mind. Walk a new route. Use your non-dominant hand to brush your teeth. The more variety you allow, the more resilient your brain becomes.

2289.articleTitle: Fuel Your Body for the Long Haul
2289.articleBodyCopy:
No one dreams of a trip to the ER. But many of us treat our bodies like we’ve got a backup in the garage.

Here’s the truth: you only get one. And how it carries you through midlife depends on daily choices—hydration, movement, and foods that actually fuel you.

Every sip of water supports your systems. Every step keeps your muscles and bones strong. Every colorful plate gives your body what it needs to stay balanced.

Think of your body like a car. What kind of fuel are you using, and when’s the last time you checked under the hood?

2290.articleBodyCopy:
Touch is a powerful form of connection. And it doesn't always need to be sexual or romantic – it can be platonic, therapeutic, or simply a way to nurture yourself. Whether it’s a hug, a massage, or even the simple touch of your own hand on your skin, these moments of connection are meaningful. What matters is consent, respect, and the openness to explore what feels good for you.

Pleasure, too, isn't just about sex or orgasm. It’s about reconnecting with your own body and experiencing the joy of sensation. As we get older, our experiences with romance and sex may change. Maybe you’re not feeling that same instant attraction you once did, or maybe you’re not partnered right now. But desire – the anticipation of pleasure – can still be part of your life.

Self-pleasure is a healthy and natural way to explore your body, whether you're partnered or single. It’s about discovering new ways to feel good in your skin, such as noticing how your palm feels on your neck or the soft touch of your feet. Pleasure doesn’t have to fit into a specific box. It can simply be about the joy of feeling, without any pressure or expectations.

Ultimately, it's about expanding our understanding of touch and pleasure. You deserve to experience both, in all their forms, whether alone or with others. It’s time to redefine what feels good for you and embrace all the ways touch and pleasure can show up in your life.

2291.articleTitle: The Hidden Danger of Pulmonary DVT
2291.articleBodyCopy:
We take breathing for granted...until something makes it hard. Shortness of breath can be your body waving a red flag, and it's not something to ignore. One serious cause? A deep vein thrombosis, or DVT—a blood clot that can travel to the lungs and become a pulmonary embolism.

DVTs don’t always come out of nowhere. Risk factors include a history of smoking, hormone use (like oral contraceptives), prolonged sitting (think long flights or desk jobs), and a sedentary lifestyle. They’re more common in the lower extremities but can form elsewhere too. Look for signs like swelling, redness, and pain—especially if it’s one-sided. And don’t wait to see if it gets better. If a clot breaks loose, it could be life-threatening.

Like chest pain, symptoms that affect your ability to breathe or move should never be brushed off. DVTs can seriously impact your quality of life, and early intervention matters. Even if your primary care doctor is booked out for months, this is worth a trip to urgent care or the ER. Listen to your body. It’s trying to keep you alive.

2292.articleBodyCopy:
Yeast infections are common—but if they keep coming back, it’s time to look deeper. Most show up as itching and a cottage cheese-like discharge, but you can also have a yeast infection and something else, like a UTI or BV. 

Yeast is a fungus that thrives in warm, dark places, and it loves sugar. High blood sugar, even from undiagnosed diabetes or prediabetes, can feed yeast and throw off your vaginal pH. 

If you're getting frequent infections, ask about checking for sugar in your urine—it shouldn’t be there. Other triggers? Hormonal shifts, stress (hi, cortisol), genetics, or disrupted pH from overwashing. Stay hydrated, skip scented products, and consider probiotics. 

More than 3-4 infections a year? Time to talk to your doctor.

2293.articleBodyCopy: As we age, especially in our 40s and 50s, the pressure to keep pushing can take a toll on our energy and well-being. The “more, more, more” mindset of work culture doesn’t leave room for self-care. But self-care isn’t a luxury, it’s essential. If you're constantly stressed or feeling unfulfilled, it might be time to step back. Give yourself permission to rest, recharge, and thrive. Remember, taking care of yourself now helps you give more later.

2294.articleBodyCopy:
You’re juggling work, family, emails, errands, laundry, maybe even a leaky faucet—and somehow, you’re still expected to show up with energy and a smile? No wonder your brain won’t shut off at night.

We’re getting real about self-care—not the bubble bath kind (although those are nice too), but the foundational kind that starts with rest. When we don’t sleep, everything else suffers—our immune system, our patience, our energy, our ability to cope. Sleep isn’t a luxury, it’s our body’s original recovery plan.

Chronic sleep disruption chips away at your health. Reclaim rest—starting with your breath. Explore some practical, science-backed ways to tap into your body’s “rest and digest” system and calm that racing mind.

Because here’s the thing: your to-do list can wait. Your well-being can’t.

2296.articleTitle: ACES Part 1: What’s Your ACEs Score?
2296.articleBodyCopy: Trauma doesn’t always look like we expect it to. For some, it’s a major event. For others, it’s something subtle but persistent. But no matter how it shows up, the body remembers. ACEs—or Adverse Childhood Experiences—are events that can happen before age 18. Things like losing a parent, feeling unloved, or experiencing abuse. Your score isn’t just a number-it’s a window into how early life experiences may still be showing up in your health, relationships, and stress levels today. That’s why understanding your ACEs score is so important—it can help explain why you feel the way you do, and open the door to healing. In this video, we talk about how trauma can be stored in the body, how it impacts your long-term health, and what healing can look like—from self-care and therapy to somatic work and breath practices. If you’ve ever wondered why certain things feel so hard, or why your nervous system is always on high alert, this is a good place to start. Take the quiz to find your ACEs score. Learn more about the original Kaiser ACE Study. Your past doesn’t have to define your future—but acknowledging it is a powerful first step.

2297.articleTitle: ACES Part 2: The Hidden Impact of Trauma
2297.articleBodyCopy:
Can early life trauma affect your health decades later?

Yes! And often in ways that are hard to pin down. In Part 2 of our ACES & Trauma series, we explore how unprocessed childhood stress can disrupt the nervous system, triggering physical symptoms in adulthood.

These responses aren’t random, they’re the body’s way of expressing stored stress that was never fully processed. Understanding this mind-body connection isn’t just helpful for your own healing, it’s also essential for supporting others who carry trauma you may not recognize.

Learn how trauma manifests, and how the body begins to heal through release.

2298.articleTitle: ACES Part 3: Listening to the Body
2298.articleBodyCopy:
Ever felt a tight chest, upset stomach, or a lump in your throat, with no clear physical cause? In Part 3 of our ACES & Trauma series, we explore how unprocessed trauma—especially from early life—can become trapped in the body, showing up as tension, pain, or even a voice that falters when it tries to speak.

Trauma isn't always loud. Sometimes it whispers through GI symptoms, shallow breathing, or chronic discomfort. But when we slow down and listen—through practices like body scans, mindful breathing, or somatic therapy—we start to notice where our energy is stuck and where it’s asking for release.

These subtle signs are your body’s way of saying: “There’s still something here to heal.” Stored trauma communicates through the body. Awareness, movement, and emotional release can begin to set it free.

2299.articleBodyCopy:
Menopause shakes things up-and that includes your urinary tract. Lower estrogen can change your body’s defenses, making infections sneakier and symptoms tougher to shake.

Let's break down what’s really going on, how to spot the signs early, and why treatments might need to shift as hormones change. From hydration tips to the surprising role of vaginal estrogen and cranberry juice, you’ll get clear, practical advice to keep your urinary health strong through the midlife transition.

2300.articleTitle: ADHD & Perimenopause: Why Your Brain Feels Like It's on Overdrive
2300.articleBodyCopy:
Ever feel like your brain is a messy desk—papers everywhere, a coffee stain in the corner, and no idea where you put that important to-do list? If you’re in your 40s or 50s and suddenly struggling more with focus, memory, and organization, you’re not alone. Many women are just now discovering they have ADHD, and perimenopause is turning up the volume on symptoms they’ve been managing for years.

For decades, ADHD was seen as a “boy’s disorder,” but for women, it often looks like missed deadlines, misplaced keys, or planners that never quite get used. Add dropping estrogen levels into the mix, and it’s like your brain’s safety net has been yanked away. Sound familiar?

Here’s the good news: You’re not just forgetful, lazy, or disorganized—you might just have an ADHD brain that’s being pushed to its limits. The even better news? There are steps you can take right now: track your symptoms, seek professional evaluation, explore treatment options, and build a support system.

You’re not failing—your brain just plays by different rules. And once you understand those rules, you can start playing to win.

2303.articleTitle: Boost Your Brain: How Exercise Fights Brain Fog
2303.articleBodyCopy:
Ladies, let’s talk about that mid-sentence brain freeze-you know, when you walk into a room and immediately forget why you're there. If perimenopause has you feeling foggy, forgetful, or just plain moody, you’re not alone! But here’s some good news: your brain has a built-in “refresh” button, and it’s called exercise.

When estrogen levels drop during perimenopause, so does a powerful brain-boosting protein called BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor). This little miracle worker keeps your memory sharp and your mood stable. But as estrogen dips, so do those mental superpowers. The result? Brain fog, mood swings, and that frustrating “what was I saying again?” moment.

The solution? Move your body! Exercise naturally ramps up BDNF production, helping your brain stay sharp and your emotions more balanced. And no, you don’t need to turn into a gym rat overnight—even just 10 minutes of walking, yoga, or some spontaneous kitchen dancing (we’ve all done it) can do wonders. Bonus points if you get your heart rate up, since exercise also helps protect against stroke and keeps your energy levels up.

So, the next time brain fog tries to take over, fight back with movement. Your brain—and everyone who listens to your stories on repeat—will thank you!

2304.articleBodyCopy:
Perimenopause is like that awkward stage of life where your body decides to shake things up—hormones are all over the place, sleep feels like a distant memory, and even your favorite sweater might start to irritate you. Suddenly, things that used to slide off your back are triggering your short fuse, whether it’s snapping at your partner, feeling frustrated with your kids, or just not tolerating things the way you once did. It’s not just you-your body is changing, and it’s time to give yourself a little more understanding and space.

When irritability strikes, it could be the hormones, a bit of physical discomfort, or just plain old exhaustion catching up with you. So, what can you do? First, take a pause before reacting. Try to breathe, and ask yourself, "What do I really need right now?" Check in with your body. Maybe you’re thirsty, tired, or hungry, and that’s making everything feel worse. Set some boundaries, too. You have every right to say no and ask for help. Lastly, consider talking to a professional, whether it's a therapist or doctor, to help manage your irritability and find solutions. Remember: Your needs are changing, and that’s perfectly okay. Be kind to yourself. Grace is your best friend during this season of life!

2305.articleBodyCopy:
Anxiety during perimenopause is a complex experience influenced by hormonal fluctuations, physical symptoms, and life transitions. Estrogen levels rise and fall unpredictably, disrupting the balance in mood regulating chemicals like serotonin and dopamine. Physical symptoms like night sweats and muscle soreness can disrupt sleep. Poor sleep quality further contributes to anxiety and irritability. Additionally, life changes like increased career demands and managing caregiving responsibilities (like children leaving the nest or caring for aging parents) add emotional stress that interacts with the biological changes happening in your body.

Explore the latest evidence-based medical treatments and lifestyle strategies for managing this common midlife experience. By understanding how brain chemistry and life stressors interact, you can create a personalized approach to managing anxiety and improving overall well-being through this transition.

2306.articleBodyCopy:
Have you been feeling unlike yourself lately? Are once-manageable tasks now draining, or have you noticed it’s harder to enjoy the things that used to bring you happiness? These could be signs of depression related to perimenopause-a common but often misunderstood experience.

During this transition, estrogen levels fluctuate dramatically. This hormone doesn’t just regulate your cycle-it helps control mood-related chemicals like serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. Estrogen also protects and supports your brain’s communication systems. Even subtle changes can cause shifts that affect your mood.

At the same time, symptoms like poor sleep, fatigue, and joint discomfort can drain your energy. Add in life stressors-like changing relationships, caregiving, or career demands-and emotional reserves get depleted fast.

Taking care of your mental and physical health is not a luxury—it’s essential. If you're struggling, talk to a provider who understands the connection between menopause and mental health.

2307.articleTitle: Let's Talk about Sex: Why Communication Matters More Than You Think
2307.articleBodyCopy:
Let’s be real-communication is one of the biggest keys to a healthy, satisfying sex life and a strong relationship. But how often are we actually talking about sex…like, really talking about it?

We’re digging into the connection between communication and sexual well-being-especially now. You’ll learn why it matters, what gets in the way, and a few simple ways to start having more open, supportive conversations about sex. Because you deserve to feel heard, connected, and confident.

2310.articleBodyCopy:
We’re often told that menopause marks the decline of our sexuality-but what if it’s actually an invitation to step into your sexual power in a whole new way?

Let's explore how menopause can be a full-body, full-soul reorganization-and a chance to redefine what sexual health and satisfaction truly mean to you. Yes, it’s normal for your sex life to ebb and flow throughout your life. But this season doesn’t have to mean shutting down. It can be a conscious choice to turn inward, ask what pleasure means to you now, and decide how you want to move forward.

You’re not losing something-you’re gaining clarity, agency, and connection. Let’s talk about how to claim it.

2311.articleBodyCopy: When was the last time you truly asked yourself: What do I want? We’re exploring what it means to seek pleasure—not just in the bedroom, but in your whole life. So many of us were never taught to prioritize our own pleasure. In fact, we may have been taught to silence it, ignore it, or feel shame around it. But this chapter of life offers a chance to rewrite the script. Together, we’ll reflect on what pleasure means to you, what might be holding you back from accessing it, and how to take small, intentional steps toward releasing shame and reclaiming desire. You don’t need to have all the answers—just the freedom to start asking the questions. And if you're curious to keep going, OMGYes is a fantastic resource to deepen this journey and break open the conversation around female pleasure. Book mentioned in this video: Want by Gillian Anderson

2312.articleBodyCopy: Have you ever brought up your perimenopause or menopause symptoms to a doctor-only to be brushed off with, “That’s just a normal part of aging” or “Try eating more protein”? You’re not alone. Self-advocacy during this transition is essential. Knowing how to speak up, ask the right questions, and find the right support can make all the difference in how you move through this season-not just physically, but emotionally and sexually, too. You deserve care that meets you where you are and helps you thrive. And if you’re looking for a provider who truly understands this phase of life, Menopause.org is a great place to find specialists trained to support you through it all.

2313.articleTitle: Mindfulness Tools for a More Connected Sex Life
2313.articleBodyCopy:
Our minds and bodies are always in conversation—and when it comes to sex, that connection becomes even more important. The thoughts we carry can shape how we feel physically, and our physical experiences can echo back into how we think, feel, and connect with others.

This piece explores how the mind-body connection shows up in sex, especially during perimenopause and menopause. You'll learn simple, grounding mindfulness tools that can help you feel more present, more connected, and more in tune—both with yourself and with your partner, emotionally and physically.

2314.articleBodyCopy:
Did you know that during perimenopause you have as much hormonal changes as a middle school girl and that on the other side of that, once you are in menopause, most women have less estrogen than their male counterparts?! Cognitive symptoms can actually be more common than the physical symptoms that we commonly associate with menopause.

We will explore the role estrogen plays in mood, how this shows up in perimenopause and menopause, and strategies for navigating this.

2315.articleBodyCopy: Desire discrepancy is one of the most common things related to sexual health that many couples navigate, yet it is rarely talked about in a meaningful way. This video explores what the different desire types are, how these differences can impact relationships, and strategies for navigating this.

2316.articleBodyCopy: We have been taught to believe that our sexual response is a physical response-but in reality, most of what dictates our ability to be “turned on” is actually a brain based response. This brain-based response can be broken down into two components-breaks (things that turn us off and move us away from sex), and accelerators (things that turn us on and move us towards sex). Explore further what breaks and accelerators are and how to pay attention to and leverage these signals to create space for more intention around sex and intimacy. Interested in learning more about how this shows up for yourself and/or your partner? Emily Nagoski’s books Come As You Are and Come Together are both great resources to check out!

2317.articleTitle: Stress, Sex, and Completing the Stress Cycle
2317.articleBodyCopy: Stress can take a serious toll on our sex drive, but here’s the twist: sex itself can be a powerful way to release some of that stress we carry. Around perimenopause and menopause, stress and intimacy can get tangled up in tricky ways. Learning how to complete what’s called the “stress cycle” can help you support both your sexual wellbeing and mental health-creating space for more ease, connection, and pleasure.

2319.articleBodyCopy: Throughout a woman’s life, periods involving great physical, hormonal, and social changes such as puberty, pregnancy, and postpartum, have been identified as “windows of vulnerability” for increased body dissatisfaction, and perimenopause and menopause are no exception to this. This video helps to explore the ways in which body image and identity show up in perimenopause and menopause and strategies for disentangling ourselves from the external worlds expectations so that we are able to redefine what we want for ourselves and our bodies.

2320.articleBodyCopy:
Getting ahead of perimenopause means you can stay strong, clear-headed, and energized-even as hormones shift. By focusing on good nutrition, strength-building, quality sleep, and stress management now, you help your body adapt smoothly.

Eating enough protein and fiber supports muscle and digestion, keeping your metabolism firing and your belly less prone to stubborn fat. Building strength-not just staying skinny-helps you feel more powerful and resilient every day.

Good sleep habits boost your energy and decision-making, while managing stress keeps your cortisol levels balanced so you don’t feel overwhelmed.

In short, prepping today means fewer surprises tomorrow—and a healthier, happier you through this whole transition. You’re investing in decades of feeling your best!

2321.articleBodyCopy:
Perimenopause is the transition from your reproductive prime into menopause-and it can feel like your body is flipping scripts daily. This phase can last for years and comes with hormone levels that spike and dip unpredictably. One day you might have brain fog, night sweats, or joint pain… and the next, feel totally fine. That erratic pattern makes it hard to diagnose, and even harder to treat if your provider doesn’t understand what’s going on.

Let's break down the basics: what perimenopause actually is, why labs aren’t always helpful, and how symptoms show up across your whole body. Plus, we’ll explore why this time is so important—because what you do now (with your lifestyle, nutrition, stress, and maybe hormones) can help you feel better today and thrive through the decades ahead. Let’s take the mystery out of the madness.

2322.articleBodyCopy: If you’ve been feeling “off” and can’t quite put your finger on it, you might be in perimenopause—the transitional phase before menopause, usually starting in your late 30s or 40s. During this time, your hormones, especially estrogen and progesterone, are all over the place, which can cause everything from mood swings and brain fog to fatigue and other physical changes. It’s a wild ride, for sure, but it’s also a chance to get ahead of the game and take care of yourself as you prepare for menopause and the years beyond.

2323.articleTitle: Beat Heart Disease Before It Starts
2323.articleBodyCopy: Heart disease is the number 1 killer of women which is more than all cancers combined. But the good news is that 80% of the time it’s preventable. At least one in five peri & post menopausal women will experience heart palpitations and this may be the first symptom that they seek care for. Perimenopause is an optimal time we can use the tools available to us to prevent heart disease. Watch this video to learn more and calculate your risk factors for heart disease here so you can get a head start on heart protection. Want to know more about the heart during this time? Watch this video from Dr. Erin Michos Don’t Go Breaking My Heart

2325.articleBodyCopy: Do your joints and muscles ache for no apparent reason? During perimenopause women have an average reduction of 10% in bone mineral density and 0.6% in muscle mass per year after menopause. These musculoskeletal issues can be due to the decline in estradiol which impacts all types of musculoskeletal tissue including bone, tendon, muscle, cartilage, ligament and adipose. These musculoskeletal symptoms include arthralgia, also known as joint pain, loss of muscle mass, loss of bone density with increased risk of fracture, increased tendon and ligament injury and progression of osteoarthritis as well as others. Seventy percent of women in the menopause transition and beyond will experience musculoskeletal symptoms and 25% will be disabled by them. There is significant evidence to show that testing, proper nutrition, resistance training, vitamin intake and/or hormone therapy can play a very big role. 2327.articleTitle: Why Treat Menopause If It’s Natural?

Hormone therapy isn’t about turning back the clock to your 20s-it’s about giving your body the support it needs now so you can feel good, stay healthy, and actually enjoy this phase of life. You’ve got decades ahead post-menopause. You deserve to live them well.

Your symptoms aren’t a personal failure or something to just put up with. Hormone therapy can be a powerful tool to help you sleep better, think clearer, feel stronger, and thrive-not just survive.

2336.articleTitle: HRT Part 1 - Hormone Therapy as an Option
2336.articleBodyCopy: Most of us grow up hearing that menopause means hot flashes and maybe some mood swings-something to just power through with herbal tea and a fan. But if you’re in your 40s or early 50s and suddenly feeling anxious, weepy, wired but exhausted, or like you’re watching life through a foggy windshield, that might actually be perimenopause. And it’s not just “getting older” or “being stressed.” It’s your hormones changing-sometimes dramatically. Here’s the truth: hormone therapy (HT) isn’t just for people drenched in night sweats. When used appropriately, HT can be a safe and powerful tool to support your brain, your sleep, your bones, and your overall quality of life. It’s not one-size-fits-all, and it’s not without nuance-but you deserve the facts, not fear. This stage of life isn’t about “gritting your teeth and getting through.” It’s about getting informed, supported, and back to feeling like yourself—confident, calm, and clear.

2337.articleTitle: HRT Part 2 - Hormone Therapy: Is It Time, Too Late, or Just Right?
2337.articleBodyCopy:
So... hormone therapy.
Is it time? Too late? Too risky? Too confusing?
Totally normal questions.

Let me just say this up front: If you’re somewhere in the perimenopause maze and wondering if hormone therapy (HT) might help, you are not behind. You’re not broken. And you definitely don’t need to figure it all out alone.

Here's the deal-this whole journey is personal. Like, Target-run-in-pajamas personal. We’re not looking for perfect hormone levels on a chart (spoiler alert: testing during perimenopause is like trying to nail Jell-O to the wall).

Perimenopause can bring all kinds of symptoms from brain fog to bloating to “why do my knees hurt now?” And while hormone therapy isn’t the answer for everyone, it can be a game-changer for some. The key is figuring out your sweet spot.

Sometimes that means starting with progesterone. Sometimes it means layering estrogen in. Sometimes it means stepping back and working on sleep, stress, and nutrition first-because hormones are powerful, but they’re not miracle workers. (Sorry, estrogen can’t fix a triple shot espresso habit.) There are lots of options, and you can mix and match based on what your body likes best.

Bottom line: hormone therapy is not one-size-fits-all. It’s not even one-size-fits-you-forever. It’s a process, and it should change as you change. So whether you’re just starting to wonder about it, or you’re deep in the weeds trying to figure out why you feel so off, know this-you deserve care that fits you.

Medications such as gabapentin may help. Supplements like vitamin D and calcium support bone health, fiber aids digestion, and magnesium can improve sleep and reduce anxiety. A balanced diet is key, but supplements can fill gaps. Always choose trusted products and work with your healthcare provider to find the best approach for your unique needs during this transition. 2339.articleBodyCopy: Testosterone isn’t just a male hormone—women produce it too, mostly in the ovaries, at levels higher than estrogen. It supports energy, mood, muscle strength, libido, memory, and skin health. During perimenopause and menopause, testosterone levels gradually decline, leading to symptoms like fatigue, brain fog, low sex drive, muscle loss, joint pain, and urinary issues. Although testosterone therapy isn’t FDA-approved for women, research shows it may help. Usually given as a low-dose gel, it requires careful evaluation, baseline testing, and monitoring by an experienced provider to avoid side effects like excess hair growth or voice changes. If these symptoms affect you, discuss testosterone with your doctor.

2391.articleTitle: Brain Health: Brain Fog and Memory Changes
2391.articleBodyCopy: Many women experience brain fog and memory changes during menopause-like forgetting names, struggling to focus, or feeling distracted. These symptoms are usually temporary and improve after menopause. Brain imaging shows menopause causes a decrease in gray matter, especially in the hippocampus (memory) and amygdala (emotion). While this sounds concerning, it’s a normal part of the transition. Some hormone therapies, especially conjugated equine estrogens (from horse urine), have been linked to increased dementia risk and are best avoided after age 60. However, women who have both ovaries removed and don’t take estrogen therapy may also have a higher dementia risk. Supporting brain health means heart-healthy habits: a Mediterranean diet, maintaining a healthy weight, and managing blood pressure. Supplements like vitamin D, omega-3s, turmeric, and coenzyme Q10 may help reduce inflammation and support cognition. A common question is: When can I stop worrying about pregnancy? Menopause means going 12 months without a period-that’s when fertility ends. But if you get a period before then, the clock resets and you need to wait another 12 months.

Contraception during perimenopause isn’t just about preventing pregnancy. Hormonal options like the pill, ring, or patch can also help ease symptoms and keep your cycles more regular.

If you’re dealing with heavy or frequent bleeding, make sure to talk to your doctor.

There are two main types of IUDs: progestin IUDs can reduce bleeding and may stop your periods, which makes it hard to tell when menopause happens; copper IUDs keep your periods but can make bleeding heavier.

2393.articleTitle: The Protective Effect of Estrogen on Your Heart
2393.articleBodyCopy: Here’s something amazing about estrogen: it helps protect your heart-especially before menopause. That’s why heart attacks are pretty rare in women under 50. Estrogen relaxes blood vessels, lowers inflammation, and boosts good cholesterol—all great for heart health. But after menopause, this natural shield fades, and heart disease risk goes up. While hormone therapy isn’t usually prescribed just to protect your heart, you can take control by knowing your numbers—like blood pressure and cholesterol—and working with your doctor to keep them in a healthy range. Eating well, staying active, and managing stress also make a big difference. Let’s explore how estrogen works and simple steps to keep your heart strong and happy for years to come! 2395.articleTitle: Hormone Therapy Explained: Risks, Benefits, and Why Timing Matters
2395.articleBodyCopy:
Hormone therapy, or HRT, usually means taking estrogen-or a combination of estrogen and progesterone, depending on whether you still have your uterus. That’s super important because estrogen alone can raise the risk of uterine cancer if your uterus is still there. Adding progesterone helps keep things safe and balanced.

There are lots of ways to take hormones, so there’s almost always an option that fits your lifestyle and preferences.

You might’ve heard about a big study from the early 2000s called the Women’s Health Initiative that made many doctors cautious about prescribing hormones. That study found increased risks of breast cancer, heart attacks, and strokes in some groups using certain types of hormones. But it’s important to know the women in that study were generally older and didn’t have severe symptoms when they started therapy.

Since then, research has shown that timing really matters-starting hormone therapy closer to menopause can actually protect your heart and reduce calcium buildup in your blood vessels. Plus, the type of hormones used matters too-the WHI study involved hormones derived from pregnant mares’ urine, not the bioidentical, plant-based hormones that are often used today.

Hormones can do more than just ease symptoms-they also support your bones, memory, and sleep. Still, major health groups recommend using hormone therapy mainly for moderate to severe symptoms or specific situations like early menopause due to ovarian removal.

So remember: hormone therapy isn’t one-size-fits-all. It’s about finding what works best for you, when to start, and choosing the right type-all with the support and guidance of your doctor.

These shifts happen because dropping estrogen levels impact brain chemicals like serotonin and norepinephrine that help regulate mood. Plus, life stress-like increased work demands, caring for aging parents, or health worries-and common sleep difficulties during this time can make mood symptoms worse.

The brain itself also undergoes changes during this transition, which can affect emotions and mood stability. For many women, hormone therapy provides relief by helping to stabilize these changes. Antidepressants such as SSRIs (like Prozac or Paxil) are another effective option to manage mood swings.

If you’re noticing mood shifts that interfere with your daily life, it’s important to talk with your healthcare provider. Together, you can explore treatment options that support both your emotional and physical health through this phase.

Key supplements such as vitamin D and calcium support bone health, while turmeric, omega-3s, and ginger can help reduce inflammation and joint discomfort. Hormone therapy may also ease symptoms, but lifestyle choices remain the foundation for lasting strength and balance through midlife and beyond. 2401.articleBodyCopy: Sleep struggles are one of the most common concerns during perimenopause and menopause. From trouble falling asleep, frequent night waking, to early morning awakenings, disrupted sleep can leave you feeling exhausted. Hormonal changes, especially declining estrogen, play a big role, and symptoms like hot flashes can interrupt rest. But it’s not just hormones-conditions like sleep apnea and restless leg syndrome can also contribute and often go undiagnosed. There’s hope beyond just toughing it out. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is considered the gold standard treatment and can help reframe your thoughts around sleep, improve habits, and reduce anxiety that keeps you awake. Other helpful steps include good sleep hygiene, regular exercise, limiting alcohol, and establishing consistent sleep schedules. Certain supplements like melatonin, calcium, vitamin D, and magnesium glycinate may also support better sleep-but always check with your doctor first. If natural strategies aren’t enough, hormone therapy with estrogen or progesterone can improve sleep quality, with progesterone often helping by promoting relaxation and drowsiness at night. Better sleep is possible-you just need the right tools and guidance. As estrogen levels drop, the tissue in and around the vagina becomes thinner, less elastic, and more prone to irritation. This can lead to dryness, pain during sex, increased urinary tract infections, and even discomfort just sitting down. Unlike other menopausal symptoms that tend to fade over time, vaginal symptoms usually worsen unless treated.

But here’s the hopeful part-these changes are absolutely treatable.

2418.articleBodyCopy: Pelvic organ prolapse can feel like it comes out of nowhere—but it doesn’t. It’s more than “just hormones”. The buffer zone is a complex concept but helps to explain why many people experience prolapse during menopause that had no apparent issues earlier in life. This information isn’t meant to scare-it’s meant to empower. Whatever your situation, you deserve care that supports your quality of life and confidence. 2420.articleBodyCopy: Imagine your core is like a giant balloon.  The top is your diaphragm (your primary breathing muscle) and the bottom are your pelvic floor muscles.  Pressing in or down on one section will impact other areas and may cause other areas to bulge out.  Using breathing as a strategy to coordinate and control pressure is a VERY important strategy to learn for prolapse recovery, long term pelvic health, and prevention of future issues.

2422.articleTitle: How Hormones Support Prolapse Symptom Relief
2422.articleBodyCopy: Menopause and perimenopause are happening BECAUSE of your hormone changes. Understanding what hormones do and how they impact your pelvic health, prolapse, and pelvic floor muscles can be a game changer for many people. Check out the detailed webinar by Dr. Emily Ruel on Estrogen Levels During Menopause to get well-prepared for your conversations with your provider. Remember, estrogen is one piece of your pelvic health puzzle—equipping yourself with the right information helps you build a plan that works for you. Articles mentioned in this video: The Menopause Society Webinar that discusses the different levels of Estrogen during the stages of menopause:Vaginal Estrogen and Pelvic Floor Muscle Function Webinar mentioned that discusses the 2001 Women's Health Initiative study: Pelvic Floor Considerations for Menopause Note: you will need to provide your email address to view the webinar

2423.articleTitle: Sexual Positions for Prolapse (And How to Enjoy Them More)
2423.articleBodyCopy: SEX IS NOT BAD FOR PROLAPSE AND DOESN’T MAKE PROLAPSE WORSE!  This segment explores some fun positions and strategies to explore to make sex not only pain-free but also pleasurable for both you and your partner!

2424.articleBodyCopy:
Your pelvic floor isn’t just one muscle-it’s a team of muscles with different roles: helping you stay dry, support your organs, and respond to pressure from movement, sneezing, or lifting. This video breaks down what pelvic floor muscle training really means and why it’s more than just squeezing.

You’ll also learn how to use gravity as a tool. We can use gravity to our advantage to HELP you or CHALLENGE you during your pelvic floor muscle training.  Gravity assisted positions are very helpful when beginning pelvic floor exercises or when you are symptomatic.  Anti-gravity positions are very helpful when you are progressing and need more challenging positions/movements. This is called gravity dosing, and it’s one of the smartest ways to approach rehab.

2425.articleTitle: Tools to Assist Pelvic Floor Muscle Training
2425.articleBodyCopy: Just like in other areas of exercise and health, there are a plethora of tools we can use to help the pelvic floor muscles do the right thing at the right time. There are tools to help reduce pain, tension, and tone of the pelvic floor muscles. There are also tools we can use to help increase activation, improve strength, and enhance coordination. Understanding what your goal is and how that tool will help you reach your goal is imperative. A pelvic floor physical therapist or occupational therapist can help guide you and create an individualized program for you.

2426.articleTitle: Types of Internal Support for Prolapse
2426.articleBodyCopy: When your pelvic floor muscles aren’t able to fully support your organs from below, internal support can help keep everything where it’s supposed to be. These are called pessaries and they are inserted INTO the vaginal canal to help hold the walls up and reduce traction on the ligaments/fascia. There are medical grade and over the counter pessaries. Internal support devices can helpful during workouts, standing for long periods, or managing daily symptoms. They can also be paired with external support to give your pelvic floor a boost from both inside and out. Some period products can also function as de facto pessaries. If inserting a finger INTO the vaginal canal feels good and reduces your symptoms, this may be a good option for you to explore with your pelvic PT, urogynecologist, or other pelvic health provider. Products mentioned in this video: Menstrual Sponge Softdisc Menstrual Discs Lena Menstrual Cup Poise Impressa Revive Bladder Support Pessary

2427.articleTitle: External Support for Your Pelvic Floor
2427.articleBodyCopy: When pressure from above (like coughing, sneezing, or jumping) pushes down on your pelvic tissues, your body needs a strong counterforce from below. Sometimes, your muscles alone can’t quite keep up. That’s where external support comes in. There are wearable pelvic floor support garments that help to counteract the forces of gravity, organ contents, and intra-abdominal pressure. These can be worn just during specific activities or all day. Some can be adjusted as needed to increase or reduce support. Use the minimum amount of compression needed for that activity to reduce or eliminate symptoms (vaginal heaviness, pressure, bulging, leaking etc.). A good self check is this: does taking a hand and lifting the perineum feel good? Does it reduce or eliminate your symptoms? If yes, external support or “perineal compression” may be a good option for you! 2806.articleTitle: The Surprising Link Between Menopause & Oral Health
2806.articleBodyCopy: Dr. Brittney Penberthy is a board-certified endodontist — and while she spends her days performing root canals, she also spends a lot of time talking to her midlife patients about something bigger: how menopause can affect oral health. In this conversation, Dr. Penberthy shares what she’s learned from years of treating women in perimenopause and postmenopause, and why changes in hormones can show up in your mouth before you notice them anywhere else. From recognizing early signs to knowing when it’s time to see a dental specialist, she offers a fresh perspective on an often-overlooked part of midlife health.

2809.articleBodyCopy: Joy Baynes, FNP, has spent nearly 20 years helping women navigate reproductive and sexual health — and in recent years, she’s focused on one stage in particular: perimenopause. Why? Because she went through it herself and knows exactly how disorienting it can feel when your body suddenly isn’t responding the way it used to. In this conversation, Joy shares the most common concerns she hears from women — from “I just don’t feel like myself” to wondering why diet and exercise routines have stopped working — and why seeing a provider who truly understands this transition can make all the difference. If you’ve ever left an appointment feeling unheard or unsure of your next step, this one will help you feel informed, validated, and ready to take charge of your midlife health.

2810.articleBodyCopy: Dr. Celia Valenzuela, OB-GYN, has been caring for women for over 20 years — from the teen years all the way through menopause. In this conversation, she breaks down why so many of us aren’t sure where to turn when symptoms start and how to take those first steps toward feeling better. We talk about who to see first, how to get the answers you need, and why knowing your own body makes all the difference. It’s honest, reassuring, and full of practical tips so you can walk into your next appointment feeling informed, supported, and ready to take charge of your health.

2811.articleBodyCopy: Kara Pettinger, LMSW, is a licensed psychotherapist with specialized training in sexual health — and she’s here to talk openly about how menopause can shift intimacy, desire, and connection. In this conversation, Kara shares how physical changes, emotional wellbeing, and relationship dynamics intertwine during midlife, and why sexual health is an essential (and often overlooked) part of overall wellness. Whether you’re navigating new challenges or simply want a deeper understanding of your body and relationships, Kara offers compassionate, practical insight that helps you approach intimacy with confidence.

2812.articleTitle: Hormones, Mental Health, and Thriving Through Midlife
2812.articleBodyCopy: Meet Dr. Alecia Greenlee, a psychiatrist specializing in reproductive psychiatry — the unique intersection of hormones and mental health throughout a woman’s life. In this interview, Dr. Greenlee shares how shifting hormones in perimenopause can impact mood, anxiety, and relationships, and why emotional competency is just as important as medical treatment. From PMS to postpartum to menopause, she offers compassionate, science-based insight into what’s happening in you

2813.articleBodyCopy:
Your hormones are shifting—and so should your nutrition. In this interview, Jennifer Woodward, functional diagnostic nutrition practitioner and integrative health expert, breaks down how what you eat can either support or stall your progress in perimenopause.

From blood sugar to inflammation to why you might need more protein than ever before, Jennifer shares practical, food-first strategies to help you feel more energized, balanced, and in control.

This isn’t a one-size-fits-all plan—it’s real talk about what works for real women in midlife.

2814.articleTitle: Pelvic Floor Health and Midlife Wellness
2814.articleBodyCopy: Your pelvic floor does more than you think—and it deserves some love, especially in midlife. In this interview, pelvic floor physical therapist and yoga teacher Anne Duch, PT, shares her decades of experience helping women navigate perimenopause and menopause with confidence. From understanding prolapse and urinary incontinence to supporting your core through every life stage, Anne’s insights will leave you informed, empowered, and ready to connect with your body in new ways.

2815.articleBodyCopy: Pelvic floor issues are common—but they’re not something you just have to live with. In this interview, Dr. Becky Allen, a seasoned pelvic floor physical therapist, shares her expertise on how pelvic health impacts everything from core strength to bladder control to overall confidence. She breaks down why pelvic floor care matters in midlife, what symptoms to watch for, and the simple steps you can take to support your body better. If you’ve ever wondered whether pelvic floor therapy could help you feel stronger and more at ease in your own skin, this conversation is a must-watch.

2816.articleBodyCopy:
What if you could move your body, calm your mind, and feel more at home in yourself—all in one conversation?

In this interview, celebrity yoga instructor and wellness expert Kristin McGee (E-RYT 500, Pilates and Meditation Specialist) shares her wisdom on building strength, finding balance, and creating a mindful movement practice that truly supports women in midlife. Whether you're navigating perimenopause, seeking stress relief, or just want to feel stronger and more centered, this chat is packed with insights and inspiration you won't want to miss.

2817.articleBodyCopy:
Kaitlin Heaney, certified fitness coach and expert contributor, shares her powerful story of transformation—from battling depression, anxiety, and a seizure disorder to becoming a thriving coach helping other women reclaim their health.

In this candid interview, Kaitlin opens up about starting exercise at 31, navigating postpartum recovery, overcoming the fear of movement after medical challenges, and how small steps like walking changed everything. Her story is proof that it’s never too late to find your strength, rebuild your confidence, and create a life you love.

Watch now and feel inspired to take that first step toward your own health journey.

2818.articleTitle: Discover Yoga That Meets You Where You Are
2818.articleBodyCopy:
In this candid conversation, Ashley sits down with Gina, founder of Balance Mom Yoga and a certified yoga instructor with years of experience helping women move through postpartum recovery, pelvic floor challenges, and now, perimenopause.

Gina shares her journey from early yoga beginnings to creating a style of practice tailored for women navigating prolapse, diastasis recti, and the shifts of menopause. They talk about real-life adjustments, what the research says about yoga easing menopausal symptoms, and how mindful movement can feel like coming home to your body again.

If you’ve ever wondered how yoga can support you through big hormonal transitions, this interview is for you.
